passages.original: ita nihil, ut dixi, ecclesiae christianae Hebraeorum testimonia conferunt, quae magis constet ex gentibus quam ex ludaeis. sane si sunt aliqua, ut fama est. Sibyllae de Christo praesagia aut Hermetis. quem • dicunt Trismegistum, aut Orphei aliorumque in gentilitate uatum, haec nos aliquanto ad fidem iuuare poterunt, qui ex gentibus efficimur christiani ; Hebraeorum uero testimonia nobis, etiamsi sint uera, ante fidem inutilia sunt, post fidem superuacua.
passages.english: So, as I said, the testimonies of the Hebrews contribute nothing to the Christian church, which consists more of gentiles than of Jews. Certainly, if there are, as rumour has it, some prophecies about Christ by the Sibyl, or by Hermes whom they call Trismegistus, or by Orpheus and other seers among the pagans, these might help us somewhat toward faith, since we are made Christians from among the gentiles; but the testimonies of the Hebrews, even if they are true, are useless to us before faith and superfluous after faith.
passages.notes: 'ludaeis' read as 'Iudaeis'; stray mark '•' before 'dicunt' omitted. The passage is Faustus' argument as quoted by Augustine.

passages.original: si quos alios gentilium reperiret de Christo aliquid praenuntiasse? sed non faceret; eos quippe sibi incognitos fassus est dicens: sane si sunt aliqua, ut fama est. Sibyllae de Christo praesagia aut Hermetis, quem dicunt Trismegistum, aut Orphei aliorumque in gentilitate uatum. horum ergo iste litteras nesciens. quandoquidem per famam putat esse aliquos tales. non eas utique legeret illi dicenti "nec prophetis credo nec Christo." quid igitur faceret?
passages.english: [Would he read] whatever other pagans he might find to have foretold something about Christ? But he would not do it; for he has admitted that they are unknown to him, saying: 'Certainly, if there are, as rumour has it, some prophecies about Christ by the Sibyl, or by Hermes whom they call Trismegistus, or by Orpheus and other seers among the pagans.' Since, then, this man does not know their writings, inasmuch as he supposes from rumour that there are some such, he certainly would not read them to that man who says, 'I believe neither the prophets nor Christ.' What, then, would he do?
passages.notes: The opening sentence is incomplete as a unit; it continues the question in the preceding context ('would Faustus perhaps read the Sibyls... or any other pagans...'), so the bracketed verb is supplied from there.
